Instruct Claude to assign a numerical severity score (1–10) to every issue and report only those scoring 8 or above.
Establish clear thresholds that separate reportable defects and security concerns from cosmetic preferences and patterns your team has already accepted.
Include the directive: 'Flag only issues where you have substantial certainty they represent actual problems.'

explanation: Option C is correct because it addresses the root cause: developers dismiss findings not because they lack confidence, but because the findings don't align with the team's actual standards. Explicitly defining what constitutes a reportable issue—versus acceptable local variation—ensures Claude focuses on genuinely relevant feedback. Options A and B attempt to filter by confidence or scoring, which doesn't solve the mismatch between technical accuracy and project relevance. Option D relies on vague instruction-following without clarifying what the team actually values, leaving the ambiguity that caused dismissals in the first place.

question: Your code review automation runs in a CI environment where initialization takes 16 seconds before analysis begins. Tracing shows the delay originates from automatic scanning for hooks, MCP servers, plugins, extensions, and cascading CLAUDE.md files across your monorepo structure. You must cut startup time while preserving enforcement of your team's standards, which live in a CLAUDE.md at the repository root. What is the best solution?

options.text: Activate --bare mode and embed all review standards directly in the -p prompt parameter for each CI run, avoiding external file dependencies.
Override the default prompt using --system-prompt-file ./CLAUDE.md, which disables automatic discovery and loads only your project rules.
Activate --bare mode and use --append-system-prompt-file ./CLAUDE.md to load your project standards while disabling all automatic discovery.
Retain standard initialization and add --exclude-dynamic-system-prompt-sections to decrease prompt variance across CI runners and boost prompt-cache efficiency.

explanation: Option C is correct because --bare mode eliminates automatic discovery overhead, and --append-system-prompt-file explicitly loads only the root CLAUDE.md without scanning for additional files. Option A embeds standards in the prompt, which is inefficient and loses the benefits of file-based configuration. Option B uses --system-prompt-file, which replaces rather than appends, potentially losing Claude Code's built-in capabilities. Option D keeps the expensive automatic discovery that causes the original 16-second delay.

question: Your team is adopting Claude Code for development tasks including generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You're configuring MCP servers to support team workflows. Your organization needs a shared airport information server accessible to everyone, and you personally want to experiment with a private weather data server that only you should access. Which MCP configuration method correctly implements these scopes?

options.text: Configure both servers in your local ~/.claude.json file.
Add the airport server to .mcp.json and the weather server to ~/.claude.json.
Add the airport server to ~/.claude.json and the weather server to .mcp.json.
Configure both servers in the project-level .mcp.json file.

explanation: Option B is correct because .mcp.json is the project-level configuration shared across team members (appropriate for the shared airport server), while ~/.claude.json is user-specific (appropriate for your personal weather server experiment). Option A puts both in the personal config, making the airport server inaccessible to teammates. Option C reverses the scopes. Option D puts both in the shared project file, exposing your experimental weather server to the entire team.

question: Your CI pipeline executes: PROMPT='You are a code reviewer.' PROMPT="$PROMPT Examine the submitted changes" PROMPT="$PROMPT for defects, security vulnerabilities, and code quality issues." claude -p \ --dangerously-skip-permissions \ --system-prompt "$PROMPT" < changes.diff The reviews run successfully and produce feedback, but Claude only comments on the piped diff—it doesn't examine related files in the repository to understand dependencies and call chains, even when changes affect widely-used functions. What modification will enable Claude to explore relevant repository files while preserving your custom review instructions?

options.text: Retain --system-prompt and add --allowedTools 'Read, Glob, Grep' because non-interactive -p mode otherwise blocks filesystem tools.
Substitute --append-system-prompt for --system-prompt so your review instructions augment Claude Code's native file-reading and navigation capabilities instead of replacing them.
Omit --system-prompt entirely and place review instructions in a root CLAUDE.md because --system-prompt disables tool use in -p mode.
Remove stdin piping and include the diff inline in the prompt string so Claude Code enters an interactive session rather than stream-processing mode.

explanation: Option B is correct because --append-system-prompt adds your instructions to Claude Code's default system prompt, which includes guidance for file-reading and code navigation. In contrast, --system-prompt replaces the entire system prompt, stripping out the built-in directives that enable tool use. Option A's --allowedTools flag doesn't exist or doesn't override the prompt-replacement behavior. Option C removes your custom instructions unnecessarily. Option D changes the invocation mode in a way that doesn't address the core issue: the system prompt replacement.

question: You are developing a document intelligence system that extracts structured data from unstructured sources, validates against schemas, and integrates with downstream applications. The system must handle anomalies gracefully and maintain accuracy. Your pipeline processes purchase orders and extracts line-item amounts, subtotals, applicable taxes, and final totals. During testing, you find that 22% of extractions show a mismatch between the sum of line-item amounts and the extracted final total—sometimes from source document defects, sometimes from model extraction errors. Downstream systems reject records with inconsistent totals. Which strategy most reliably improves extraction accuracy?

options.text: Provide few-shot examples showing purchase orders where extracted line items mathematically sum to the stated total, training the model toward consistent outputs.
Extract line items and totals separately, then apply a secondary validation step to identify and resolve inconsistencies by determining which values are most reliable.
Apply post-processing logic that rescales line-item amounts proportionally whenever their sum diverges from the stated total.
Include both a 'computed_total' field (summing extracted line items) and a 'document_total' field (from the source), then route mismatches to human review.

explanation: Option D is correct because it captures both values explicitly and flags discrepancies for human judgment, which is essential when the source document itself may contain errors. This approach preserves data integrity and allows humans to determine whether the mismatch stems from OCR failure or extraction error. Option A uses few-shot learning, which doesn't address cases where the source document is genuinely inconsistent. Option B creates a secondary model dependency without solving the fundamental ambiguity of which value is correct. Option C automatically adjusts data, introducing silent corruption when source documents are flawed and masking the true nature of errors.

question: You are developing a financial services chatbot using Claude that manages customer inquiries related to loans, account transfers, dispute resolution, and payment processing. The bot initially had access to four core MCP tools (retrieve_account, verify_transaction, initiate_transfer, file_dispute). After adding specialized capabilities for loan management (check_loan_status, calculate_interest, approve_disbursement, request_modification, adjust_rate) and payment processing (process_payment, reverse_charge, apply_fee_waiver, schedule_autopay), the tool portfolio expanded to 13 total. Recent performance metrics indicate tool invocation accuracy dropped from 85% to 68%. Error analysis shows the agent frequently confuses semantically related tools—using reverse_charge instead of apply_fee_waiver for fee corrections, and calling check_loan_status when retrieve_account already provides the necessary information. Which structural change would most directly address the semantic confusion documented in the error analysis?

options.text: Partition tools into specialized sub-agents: a "lending" agent handling loan-related operations and a "payments" agent managing transaction tools, with a dispatcher routing requests appropriately.

Merge overlapping tools into unified operations—combine reverse_charge and apply_fee_waiver into a single adjust_charges tool with a mode parameter, and integrate check_loan_status into retrieve_account with an optional loan_details flag.

Configure lazy loading for the nine new tools with deferred initialization, keeping the original four tools always available, enabling the agent to discover specialized tools only when explicitly needed.

Enhance the system prompt with detailed examples illustrating correct tool selection for each confusing pair, such as scenarios showing when apply_fee_waiver is appropriate versus when reverse_charge should be used.

explanation: The error analysis specifically identifies semantic confusion between related tools (reverse_charge vs apply_fee_waiver, check_loan_status vs retrieve_account). Partitioning tools into specialized sub-agents with a dispatcher directly addresses this by reducing the decision space within each context—the payments agent only sees payment tools, and the lending agent only sees loan tools, eliminating cross-domain confusion. While merging tools (B) might reduce total tool count, it doesn't address the fundamental problem of semantic overlap and could introduce complexity through mode parameters. Prompt engineering (D) doesn't structurally change the decision space, and lazy loading (C) doesn't help when the agent needs access to multiple specialized tools simultaneously.

question: A multi-stage research pipeline processes market analysis requests through sequential agents: a discovery agent gathers 30 sources containing 150,000 tokens of raw data, a filtering agent extracts 18,000 tokens of validated insights, and a composition agent produces a 4,000-token analytical summary. The final reporting agent must now generate client-ready output with proper source attribution. What context-management approach best combines thoroughness with operational efficiency?

options.text: Transmit a compressed overview of all upstream stages that retains essential conclusions while attributing findings to source identifiers only.
Forward the composition agent's summary alongside a structured reference table that links specific insights to their originating source URLs and supporting text passages.
Send only the composition agent's summary and employ a downstream citation-matching system to connect conclusions to sources and embed references after report finalization.
Transmit the entire accumulated context spanning all prior agent outputs and intermediate processing steps.

explanation: The correct answer balances completeness and efficiency by pairing the refined synthesis with a structured source index, enabling the final agent to cite claims accurately without processing redundant raw data. Option A loses critical source linkage information. Option C defers citation matching to post-processing, risking citation errors and requiring additional pipeline stages. Option D wastes context tokens by including unrefined intermediate outputs that the final agent doesn't need.

question: Your organization has deployed Claude Code for automated technical review of pull requests in a microservices architecture. The review system processes each PR using a single API call with a fixed prompt that includes only the modified code sections and full text of changed files. Unchanged files are excluded from analysis. Engineering teams report that reviews frequently overlook integration issues—for instance, a PR updates a service's API contract, but the review fails to catch consumer services in unmodified files that depend on the old contract. Incident analysis attributes 40% of production defects traced to reviewed PRs to these cross-module integration gaps. How should the review system be redesigned to address this gap?

options.text: Construct a precomputed call-graph and include all files within three dependency edges of any modified file.
Augment the prompt with instructions to identify external dependencies and reason through potential impacts on code paths that are not visible in the current diff.
Implement the review as a multi-turn agentic workflow that can navigate the codebase, follow references, and validate cross-module compatibility before concluding.
Execute multiple review iterations—one focused on each changed file paired with its immediate dependents—then consolidate results and remove duplicate findings.

explanation: The correct answer leverages agentic capabilities to dynamically explore dependencies and verify integration points, rather than relying on static analysis or prompt engineering. This interactive approach can discover and reason through complex cross-file impacts that a single-pass review cannot. Option A requires maintaining an accurate dependency graph that may be incomplete or stale. Option B asks the model to reason about unseen code, which it cannot do without actually reading those files. Option D is more thorough than static inclusion but still depends on pre-identifying dependents, missing transitive or indirect impacts.

question: Your team is building a codebase exploration platform powered by Claude that assists developers in navigating unfamiliar projects, understanding architectural patterns, generating scaffolding code, and executing maintenance tasks. The platform leverages Claude's native capabilities—Read, Write, Bash, Grep, and Glob—alongside MCP server integrations. You are implementing a vulnerability-scanning feature that requires engineers to identify all instances of a risky function call such as exec() throughout the entire codebase. Which tool is most appropriate for this content-search objective?

options.text: Apply Glob with a pattern like **/exec* to enumerate matching files, then sequentially read each identified file.
Execute Grep with the regular-expression pattern exec\( to scan all files in the repository simultaneously.
Open the primary entry point and systematically trace through import paths to determine where exec() could be invoked.
Run Bash with a command such as find . -type f | xargs grep exec and parse the output for matching lines.

explanation: Grep is the purpose-built tool for searching file contents by pattern across a codebase, making it the most efficient and direct approach for locating all instances of a specific function call. Option A wastes effort by using Glob (designed for filename matching) and requires sequential file reads. Option C cannot discover all occurrences without reading every file and tracing all possible paths. Option D replicates Grep's functionality through Bash but is less direct and more error-prone than using the dedicated search tool.

question: Performance monitoring indicates that user requests like "provide an overview of key findings from our analysis" experience latency exceeding 45 seconds. Root-cause analysis shows the orchestrator agent initiates a specialized summarization subagent for every such request, transferring more than 90,000 tokens of previously gathered analysis results. The orchestrator already maintains these analysis results in its own context window from managing the prior research workflow. What is the most effective optimization for reducing response latency on these follow-up requests?

options.text: Precompute and persistently store multi-level summaries whenever new analysis data becomes available.
Activate prompt caching on the summarization subagent to minimize the computational cost of repeatedly processing the same analysis dataset.
Empower the orchestrator to directly fulfill routine summarization requests using its cached context, invoking the subagent only for sophisticated or nuanced analyses.
Activate the subagent with a reduced context window and permit it to retrieve specific analysis sections from the orchestrator as required.

explanation: The correct answer recognizes that straightforward summarization can be handled by the orchestrator using its existing context, avoiding unnecessary subagent invocation and data transfer overhead. This is the most direct path to reduced latency for routine requests. Option A adds complexity through precomputation but doesn't eliminate the subagent call. Option B reduces per-call overhead but still incurs the latency of spawning the subagent and transferring large context. Option D still requires subagent invocation and on-demand context retrieval, which adds latency compared to using the orchestrator's cached knowledge directly.

question: Your code review system processes pull requests through a single API request, providing the model with diffs and full text of modified files while excluding unmodified files. Reviews are delivered asynchronously without blocking PR merging. Your team has observed that reviews frequently overlook issues related to impacts across multiple files—for instance, when a method signature changes, the system fails to detect usages of the old signature in unrelated modules. Incident retrospectives indicate that such cross-module issues represent 35% of post-deployment failures from reviewed PRs. Which modification would most substantially improve your review system?

options.text: Restructure the review process as a bounded agentic workflow where the model can use tools to fetch files and query the repository, enabling it to trace dependencies and validate cross-module consistency.
Enhance the prompt with explicit chain-of-thought guidance instructing the model to enumerate all external dependencies in the changes and reason through potential impacts on consuming code.
Apply static analysis to construct a call-graph of affected code, then augment the prompt with all files reachable within two levels of the dependency tree from any modified file.
Execute multiple review passes in parallel, each examining a changed file alongside its immediate reverse-dependencies, then consolidate findings through a final aggregation pass.

explanation: The core issue is that a single static API call with fixed context cannot discover cross-file impacts that require active exploration. An agentic workflow allows the model to iteratively fetch files, follow references, and verify consistency across the codebase—fundamentally solving the problem of missing cross-file bugs. Chain-of-thought prompting (B) and dependency graphs (C) remain passive and cannot adapt to unexpected call patterns, while parallel passes (D) still lack the dynamic exploration needed to find all callers.

question: Your multi-agent system uses AgentDefinition configurations for four specialized subagents, each with appropriate descriptions, system prompts, and scoped tool access. During integration testing, you observe that the coordinator agent correctly reasons about delegation—it produces statements like, "I will request the data-retrieval agent to fetch the necessary information"—yet the subagents never actually execute. The coordinator then proceeds as if delegation succeeded, working with incomplete data. System logs report no errors. What is the most probable explanation?

options.text: The AgentDefinition objects are properly configured, but the coordinator's system prompt does not enumerate the names and purposes of the available subagents.
The coordinator's allowedTools list is missing " Agent " (or " Task " in earlier SDK versions), preventing it from invoking the core tool needed to instantiate and run subagents.
Subagent sandboxing prevents task descriptions from propagating to subagents without explicit context-sharing settings in ClaudeAgentOptions.
The coordinator's token budget is insufficient, causing subagent invocation syntax to be truncated before the agent-type parameter is fully specified.

explanation: The coordinator is reasoning correctly about delegation but subagents never execute—this is a tooling problem, not a reasoning or context problem. The coordinator cannot invoke subagents without the " Agent " (or " Task ") tool in its allowedTools configuration, which is the mechanism that spawns subagent execution. Without this tool, the model can only simulate delegation in its reasoning. System prompt enumeration (A) is helpful but not required for execution; context isolation (C) would cause different symptoms; token limits (D) would truncate output, not prevent execution entirely.

question: You are developing a customer service agent using the Claude Agent SDK for handling returns, billing inquiries, and account management. The agent accesses your systems via Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (retrieve_customer_info, find_order_details, process_refund, route_to_specialist). You aim for 80%+ same-call resolution while reliably escalating unresolvable cases. In production, when complex billing issues require 7+ tool interactions, the agent sometimes reaches its max_turns threshold after collecting information but before either completing the resolution or escalating. You must ensure every customer session terminates with either a successful resolution or a specialist handoff, regardless of how the agent loop concludes. Which strategy guarantees this outcome?

options.text: Implement a pre-execution hook that monitors tool call count and forces loop termination with automatic escalation once the agent consumes 80% of its available turns.

Decompose the workflow into two sequential agents—the first gathers information using retrieve_customer_info and find_order_details, then passes results to a second agent that handles process_refund or route_to_specialist, each with independent turn allocations.

Add wrapper logic that monitors the agent's completion status after each loop termination—if the loop ends without resolution or escalation, invoke route_to_specialist programmatically with the full conversation history and collected results.
Modify the system prompt to instruct the agent to invoke route_to_specialist with a summary of findings whenever it recognizes it cannot achieve resolution with its remaining available turns.

explanation: The guarantee requires orchestration-layer control, not agent-level instructions or pre-emptive termination. Option C is the only approach that ensures escalation occurs regardless of how the agent loop ends—whether it completes, runs out of turns, or encounters other termination conditions. The pre-hook (A) is too aggressive and may escalate solvable cases; sequential agents (B) still lack the guarantee; and system prompt instructions (D) rely on the agent recognizing its state, which fails when the loop terminates unexpectedly.

question: You are implementing a collaborative research system using the Claude Agent SDK with a coordinator and specialized subagents: one performs web research, one extracts and analyzes documents, one identifies cross-source patterns, and one compiles final reports. The system investigates topics and generates comprehensive, well-sourced reports. During processing of a 28-document corpus, the pipeline fails after handling 12 documents. At that point, the web-research subagent had located sources, the document-analysis subagent had partially extracted data, and the pattern-synthesis subagent had begun identifying connections. You must resume without duplicating prior work or degrading the quality of previously discovered insights. Which state-preservation strategy best maintains both accuracy of prior findings and efficiency of context usage during recovery?

options.text: Store all subagent outputs in a vector database. On restart, each subagent uses semantic similarity search to retrieve its prior findings.

Have each subagent export its results in structured format to a shared location. When resuming, the coordinator reads the manifest and injects relevant prior outputs into each subagent's initial context.
Have each subagent maintain its own persistent state file and automatically reload it at session start.
Archive the coordinator's full conversation history containing all delegation requests and subagent responses, then provide this history to subagents upon resumption.

explanation: Structured exports (B) balance fidelity and efficiency by preserving exact prior results while allowing selective injection into new contexts, avoiding redundant reprocessing. Vector search (A) introduces lossy approximation that may degrade accuracy; independent state files (C) lack coordination and may cause inconsistencies; and providing the full conversation log (D) to subagents wastes context on irrelevant coordinator-to-subagent exchanges rather than injecting only the specific results needed for continuation.

question: You are creating a data extraction system using Claude for parsing unstructured documents. The system extracts structured information, validates output against JSON schemas, and ensures high accuracy. It must handle variations gracefully and work seamlessly with downstream systems. Your pipeline extracts data from restaurant menus, outputting structured JSON with fields for dish names, descriptions, prices, and dietary classifications. Menu sources exhibit inconsistent formatting—prices appear as "$12.99" or "12.99" or "12", and dietary information is presented as symbols, abbreviations, or full text. What is the most robust approach?

options.text: Make separate extraction calls for each field type to ensure uniform processing of each category.
Define a detailed output schema and embed format standardization rules directly in the extraction prompt.
Run multiple extraction passes per document and choose the format variant that appears most frequently across attempts.
Extract all data in raw form and apply format standardization in post-processing logic after receiving Claude's response.

explanation: Option B is correct because Claude excels at following detailed instructions and schemas in a single prompt, making it the most efficient and robust approach. By embedding format standardization rules directly in the extraction prompt alongside the output schema, you leverage Claude's ability to understand context and produce consistently formatted output in one pass. Option D adds unnecessary complexity and latency by requiring post-processing logic, while option A creates inefficiency with multiple API calls, and option C wastes resources with redundant extraction attempts without addressing the root cause of format inconsistency.

question: You are developing an intelligent code assistant using the Claude Agent SDK to help teams maintain and enhance their software systems. The assistant can leverage built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and integrates with Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. A development team submits two requests: ● Request A: "Update all import statements from the old 'utils' module to the new 'helpers' module across the codebase." ● Request B: "Refactor the authentication system to implement OAuth 2.0 with proper token refresh, session management, and comprehensive security logging." For which request would implementing a structured multi-phase approach (such as discover # design # validate # execute with checkpoints) provide the most substantial improvement in solution quality?

options.text: Neither request would benefit from this structured approach
Request A, the import statement update task
Both requests would benefit equally from the multi-phase workflow
Request B, the authentication system refactoring task

explanation: Complex, high-impact refactoring tasks like authentication system redesign benefit significantly from structured multi-phase workflows that allow for analysis, design review, and validation before implementation. In contrast, straightforward mechanical tasks like import statement updates are deterministic and benefit less from elaborate planning. The multi-phase approach enables the agent to catch architectural issues, security concerns, and design flaws early, preventing costly mistakes in critical systems.

question: You are constructing a code review automation system using the Claude Agent SDK to streamline developer workflows. The system leverages built-in tools—Read, Write, Bash, Grep, and Glob—and integrates with Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. Development teams regularly need the agent to correlate pull request changes with requirements from their project management system during reviews—retrieving requirement descriptions, acceptance criteria, and team discussions. Currently this process requires manual copying of requirement details into each conversation. The organization wants the agent to retrieve this project management data automatically. Which approach best enables this capability?

options.text: Use the Bash tool with curl commands to invoke the project management platform's REST API, handling authentication and JSON parsing within the agent workflow
Develop a specialized MCP server that wraps the project management API with tools tailored to the organization's specific review and requirements-tracking patterns
Periodically export requirements to JSON files stored in the repository that the agent accesses using the Read tool
Connect a pre-built MCP server for the project management platform that provides standardized tools for accessing requirements, discussions, and metadata

explanation: Leveraging an existing, pre-built MCP server for the project management platform is the most effective approach because it provides discoverable, standardized tool interfaces optimized for common workflows, eliminating the need for custom API handling or manual data export. While direct API calls via Bash are possible, they require manual authentication and parsing, creating maintenance burden. Custom MCP servers are valuable for specialized needs, but reusing existing servers reduces development overhead. Exporting to files creates staleness issues and defeats the purpose of automation.
